key_terms.meaning: C = C<sub>mat</sub> + C<sub>mach</sub> + C<sub>weld</sub> + C<sub>over</sub> + C<sub>setup</sub>/N
S<sub>yt</sub>/ρ and E/ρ: merit indices for light ties
upper − lower limit; smallest hole − largest shaft
k = 1 + √(1 + 2h/δ<sub>st</sub>); k = 2 for a sudden load
σ = My/I = M/Z; Z = bh²/6, πd³/32
δ = PL/(AE); θ = TL/(GJ); beam δ = PL³/(48EI), PL³/(3EI)

takeaways: Design is a loop from need to production; the specification is the test that ends it, and the concept stage fixes most of the cost.
Choose a material by sizing the part in each candidate for strength and stiffness, then comparing mass and cost; heat treatment raises strength but never E.
Preferred numbers are geometric series (R5 to R40); limits and fits make parts interchangeable, and the hole-basis system keeps the tools few.
The failure mode picks the strength: S<sub>yt</sub> for ductile parts, S<sub>ut</sub> for brittle ones; the factor of safety covers uncertainty and codes set its minimum.
A suddenly applied load doubles the stress; a falling weight multiplies it by 1 + √(1 + 2h/δ<sub>st</sub>), often by hundreds.
P/A, My/I and Tr/J give the three basic stresses; bending and direct stresses add, but shear combines with them only through principal stresses.
An offset load adds a moment Pe; the principal stresses and Mohr's circle turn any plane stress state into its largest and smallest normal stresses.
Every part must pass both a strength check and a stiffness check; long shafts and slender beams are usually sized by stiffness.
In hooks and C-frames the neutral axis moves inward and the inner fibre carries the peak stress, a third or more above the straight-beam value.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the design procedure and its factors, material selection with designations, preferred numbers and fits, and factor of safety as theory questions, and for numerical problems on combined bending and torsion with principal stresses, eccentric loading and curved beams (crane hooks and C-frames). Some syllabi set this unit together with theories of failure, stress concentration and design for fluctuating loads; those questions are in failure theories and fatigue design.

bank.q: Explain the general procedure of machine design, and discuss the factors that influence the design of a machine element.
outline: stages from need to production, with feedback
specification as the exit test
factors: load, kinematics, material, form, standard parts, workshop, batch, cost, safety, environment, maintenance, ergonomics
an example decision for each factor
cost per piece with setup shared over the batch

answer.text: Design is the creation of plans for a machine or part that does a stated job safely and economically. It is a loop of decisions, each checked against a written specification.
Recognition of need. A customer, market survey or breakdown report shows a job done badly or at high cost: for example, a fan that must hang from a brick wall.

Specification. The need is written in numbers: load (8 kg fan, 78.48 N), life (5 years), batch (200 pieces), price ceiling (₹250), environment (coastal air), codes. Each target also states how it will be verified.

Synthesis. Two or three concepts or mechanisms are sketched (bent flat bar, rolled angle, welded T) and compared. Most of the cost is fixed here, because the concept fixes the material family and the process.
Analysis of forces on each element from the mechanism and its duty, then selection of material and design of elements: sizes from stress and deflection checks with a factor of safety.

Modification: sizes are rounded to preferred sizes and changed for manufacture, assembly and appearance. Detailed drawing fixes every dimension, tolerance and finish. A prototype is built and tested; a failure sends the team back to the concept or the sizes. Production follows with process sheets and inspection.
Factors that influence design (one decision for the fan bracket each):

head: Factor
What it decides
rows: Steady weight with mild vibration: static check plus stiffness
No moving parts in the bracket
Welding and milling only; no castings
Galvanise; slotted holes for one fitter

answer.text: Cost and batch size:
answer.pre:
C = C<sub>mat</sub> + C<sub>mach</sub> + C<sub>weld</sub> + C<sub>over</sub> + C<sub>setup</sub>/N
Fan bracket: 105 + 55 + 40 + 30 + 2000/200 = ₹240 ≤ ₹250
Casting route: 120 + 60,000/200 = ₹420 (cheaper only above about 528 pieces)

answer.text: Conclusion. The procedure is iterative; the factors conflict (strength against mass, cost against tolerance) and the specification decides when the balance is good enough.

bank.q: Explain how materials are selected for machine elements on the basis of their mechanical properties. Give the Indian designations of plain carbon steel, alloy steel and cast iron with an example of each.
outline: properties: yield and ultimate strength, E, ductility, toughness, resilience, hardness, fatigue, creep
other properties: density, corrosion, machinability, weldability, cost
designations 40C8, 40Cr4, FG 200, SG 500/7
procedure: screen, size for strength and stiffness, rank
weighted-point method with a short calculation

answer.text: Strength: yield strength Syt, where permanent deformation starts, for ductile parts; ultimate tensile strength Sut for brittle parts. Stiffness: modulus of elasticity E; all steels have E of about 200 to 210 GPa, so heat treatment does not reduce deflection.

Ductility (elongation above about 5 % means ductile), toughness (energy to fracture, for shock), resilience (elastic energy, Syt²/2E per unit volume; 0.156 MJ/m³ for mild steel with 250 MPa and 200 GPa), hardness (wear), fatigue strength (repeated loads) and creep strength (high temperature).
Other properties: density for mass, corrosion resistance, machinability, weldability, castability and cost per kilogram.

Designations (Indian Standards). Plain carbon steel 40C8: 0.40 % carbon, about 0.8 % manganese. Alloy steel 40Cr4: 0.40 % carbon, about 1 % chromium. Grey cast iron FG 200: minimum tensile strength 200 MPa. Spheroidal graphite iron SG 500/7: 500 MPa and 7 % elongation.

Typical choices: mild steel for welded brackets and frames; medium-carbon or alloy steel, hardened and tempered, for shafts, gears and bolts; grey cast iron for machine beds and housings (strong in compression, damps vibration); aluminium alloy for light parts; bronze for bushes; nylon for quiet, light gears.

Procedure. (1) Write the function and the failure mode. (2) Screen out materials that cannot work. (3) Size the part in each candidate for strength and for stiffness; the larger section governs. (4) Compare the sized parts on mass and cost, then on making.
Example of sizing: a 500 mm tie, 20 kN, n = 2 on yield, stretch ≤ 0.6 mm.

Weighted-point method. Each property is scaled out of 100 (value/best for larger-is-better, lowest/value for cost), multiplied by its weight (weights add to 1) and summed. For a coastal bracket with weights strength 0.25, stiffness 0.15, cost 0.35, corrosion 0.25 the totals are mild steel 77.6, stainless steel 67.3 and aluminium 57.2.

Manufacturing properties often decide between candidates that pass the strength screen: castability for complex housings (cast iron, aluminium), weldability for fabricated frames (low-carbon steel), machinability for turned parts (free-cutting steels, brass), and hardenability for gears and shafts (alloy steels).
Conclusion. No single property decides; the material is chosen for the property set that matches the failure mode, then confirmed by size, mass and cost.

bank.q: What are preferred numbers? Explain the R5, R10, R20 and R40 series and derived series. Define tolerance, allowance and fundamental deviation, and explain the three types of fit and the hole-basis system.
outline: geometric series, ISO 3, ratios 1.585, 1.259, 1.122, 1.059
R5 and R10 values; derived series R10/3
basic size, limits, tolerance, deviation, fundamental deviation, IT grade
clearance, transition and interference fits with zone sketch or values
hole-basis versus shaft-basis and why hole-basis is preferred

answer.text: Preferred numbers are standard values arranged in geometric series (ISO 3), used for sizes and ratings so that a range is covered by few, evenly spaced variants.
Basic series:

Equal ratio steps give the same relative step (about 26 % in R10) at every size. A derived series takes every p-th term: R10/3 gives 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Example: six press sizes from 10 to 100 kN need q⁵ = 10, q = 1.585, so the R5 values 10, 16, 25, 40, 63, 100 kN.

Terms. Basic size: the size named on the drawing. Limits: the largest and smallest permitted sizes. Tolerance = upper limit − lower limit. Deviation = limit − basic size (ES, EI for holes; es, ei for shafts). Fundamental deviation: the deviation nearer the basic size, given by the letter. IT grade: the number that sets the tolerance width (IT6 = 10i, IT7 = 16i, with i = 0.45∛D + 0.001D μm).
Allowance = smallest hole − largest shaft: the minimum clearance (or, if negative, the maximum interference).
Types of fit, with the 25 mm zones (μm): H7 hole 0 to +21.

head: Fit
Shaft zone (μm)
Result
rows: Clearance 7 to 41 μm: always a gap
From 19 μm clearance to 15 μm interference

answer.text: Hole-basis system: all holes are H (EI = 0) and the shaft letter gives the fit. It is preferred because holes are made with fixed-size drills and reamers and checked with plug gauges, so one set of tools serves every fit at a size. Shaft-basis system: all shafts are h (es = 0) and the hole varies (G7/h6); it suits a long bright bar carrying several parts.
Conclusion. Preferred numbers keep the number of sizes small; limits and fits make the parts of different makers interchangeable with a planned clearance or grip.

bank.q: Discuss the modes of failure of machine parts. Explain the factor of safety, the factors that govern its choice and typical values, and the role of design codes and standards.
outline: modes: yield, fracture, deflection, fatigue, buckling, wear, corrosion, creep
n for ductile and brittle materials
factors: load and material uncertainty, stress analysis, consequence, service conditions
typical values and margin of safety
codes and standards with examples; partial factors

answer.text: Failure means the part can no longer do its job safely. Modes: yielding (ductile parts at Syt), fracture (brittle parts at Sut), excessive deflection or twist, fatigue under repeated stress, buckling of slender struts, wear of sliding surfaces, corrosion and creep at high temperature.
Factor of safety n = failure stress/allowable stress:
answer.pre:
Ductile:  σ<sub>allow</sub> = S<sub>yt</sub>/n
Brittle:  σ<sub>allow</sub> = S<sub>ut</sub>/n
Safe when working stress ≤ σ<sub>allow</sub>; margin of safety = n − 1

answer.text: Why it is needed: loads are estimated, strengths scatter between batches, stress formulas idealise the geometry, workmanship varies, and failure may injure people or stop a plant.

Factors governing its value: how well the load is known (steady or shock), how reliable the material is (rolled steel or casting), the accuracy of the analysis, the consequence of failure, the service environment and the cost of extra material.
Typical values: steady loads on ductile steel 1.5 to 2 on yield; brittle materials 3 to 4 on ultimate; shock loads 3 or more; lifting gear and pressure vessels as their codes require.
Example: a tie of 250 mm² carries 45 kN; Syt = 280 MPa; n = 2.5.
answer.pre:
σ<sub>allow</sub> = 280/2.5 = 112 MPa
σ = 45,000/250 = 180 MPa > 112 MPa   → unsafe (actual n = 1.56)
A needed = 45,000/112 = 401.8 mm² → 25 mm bar: σ = 91.7 MPa, n = 3.05

answer.text: Standards fix sizes, materials and tests for interchangeability (ISO 3 preferred numbers, ISO 286 limits and fits; IS 1570 designation of steels, IS 919 limits and fits, IS 2062 structural steel). Codes set enforceable design rules for safety: load cases, methods, minimum factors and tests, such as the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code.
Limit-state codes split the single factor into a resistance factor φ ≤ 1 and load factors γ ≥ 1, checking φR ≥ ΣγQ, so that loads and strengths with different scatter get their own margins.
A second check for a brittle part: an FG 200 cast-iron link with 12 kN and n = 4 has σallow = 200/4 = 50 MPa, needs 240 mm², and a 16 mm square (256 mm², 46.9 MPa) gives an actual factor of 4.27.
Conclusion. The failure mode chooses the strength, the uncertainty chooses n, and the code sets the minimum; a code-compliant part can still fail in a mode the code does not cover.

bank.q: Calculate the limits of the fit 50 H8/f7 and find the maximum and minimum clearance. The diameter step is 30 to 50 mm. Use i = 0.45∛D + 0.001D μm, IT8 = 25i, IT7 = 16i, and for the f shaft es = −5.5D<sup>0.41</sup> μm.
outline: geometric mean D
tolerance unit i
IT8 and IT7
hole limits
shaft fundamental deviation and limits
clearances and type of fit

answer.text: Given: basic size 50 mm, hole H8, shaft f7, step 30 to 50 mm.
Geometric mean of the step and tolerance unit:
Standard tolerances:
Hole H8: the lower deviation is zero.
answer.pre:
EI = 0, ES = +39 μm
Hole: 50.000 mm to 50.039 mm

answer.text: Shaft f7: the fundamental deviation is the upper deviation.
Clearances:
answer.pre:
Maximum clearance = 50.039 − 49.950 = 0.089 mm
Minimum clearance = 50.000 − 49.975 = 0.025 mm (the allowance)

answer.text: Summary table:

Why these steps. The standard tolerance grows with size only as the cube root of D, because a larger part is not proportionally harder to make; using the geometric mean of the step gives one value for every size from 30 to 50 mm. The letter f puts the shaft zone wholly below the zero line, and the H hole wholly above it, so the zones can never overlap.

Zone sketch (deviations in μm about the zero line at 50.000 mm): hole H8 from 0 to +39 above the line; shaft f7 from −25 to −50 below it. The gap between the top of the shaft zone (−25) and the bottom of the hole zone (0) is the allowance, 25 μm.

On the shop floor the limits become gauge sizes: the hole is checked with a GO plug of 50.000 mm and a NO-GO plug of 50.039 mm; the shaft with a GO snap gauge of 49.975 mm and a NO-GO snap gauge of 49.950 mm. Any hole and any shaft that pass their gauges will assemble with a clearance between 25 and 89 μm.

Check: maximum − minimum clearance = 0.089 − 0.025 = 0.064 mm = hole tolerance + shaft tolerance = 0.039 + 0.025. Both clearances are positive, so 50 H8/f7 is a clearance fit on the hole-basis system, suitable for a running fit such as a shaft in a plain bearing.

bank.q: A load of 1 kN falls through 20 mm onto a collar at the lower end of a vertical steel rod 2 m long and 20 mm in diameter; E = 200 GPa. Find the maximum stress and extension in the rod, the strain energy stored, and the stress if the same load were applied suddenly and gradually.
outline: area, static stress and static extension
impact factor from the energy balance
maximum stress and extension
energy check
sudden and gradual comparison

answer.text: Data in N and mm: W = 1000 N, h = 20 mm, L = 2000 mm, d = 20 mm, E = 200,000 N/mm².
Area and static values (the load applied gradually):
Energy balance. Loss of potential energy = strain energy at the lowest point: W(h + δ) = σ²AL/(2E). With δ = σL/E this gives the impact factor:
Maximum stress and extension:
answer.pre:
σ<sub>max</sub> = kσ<sub>st</sub> = 36.46 × 3.183 = 116.1 MPa
δ<sub>max</sub> = kδ<sub>st</sub> = 36.46 × 0.03183 = 1.161 mm

answer.text: Strain energy stored, two ways:
Comparison:
Check by the approximate formula (h ≫ δst): σ ≈ √(2EWh/(AL)) = √(2 × 200,000 × 1000 × 20/(314.16 × 2000)) = 112.8 MPa, within 3 % of the exact 116.1 MPa, as expected when δmax is small beside h.

Assumptions. The collar and the support are rigid, no energy is lost at impact (the weight does not bounce or deform), the stress is uniform along the rod at the instant of largest stretch, and the rod stays elastic. Real impacts lose some energy, so the result is on the safe side.

Design remark. For mild steel with Syt = 250 MPa the rod is safe against yield with an actual factor of 250/116.1 = 2.15. Since σmax ≈ √(2EWh/(AL)), the impact stress depends on the volume AL of the rod: doubling the length to 4 m, or doubling the area, cuts it by √2 to about 82 MPa. Under a steady load only the area would matter; under impact every millimetre of elastic length helps.
Answer: σmax = 116.1 MPa, δmax = 1.161 mm, U = 21.2 J; a 20 mm drop multiplies the gradual stress by 36.5 and the sudden-load stress by 18.2.

bank.q: A 50 mm solid shaft transmits 30 kW at 500 rpm. At the critical section it carries a bending moment of 1.2 kN·m and an axial compressive thrust of 10 kN. Find the principal stresses and the maximum shear stress at the worst point of the surface, and the angle of the principal planes. Draw Mohr's circle.
outline: torque from power
bending, axial and torsional stresses
worst point where bending and axial stress add
principal stresses, maximum shear, angle
Mohr's circle with values
check on the other side

answer.text: Torque:
Stresses at the surface (d = 50 mm, d³ = 125,000 mm³):
answer.pre:
Bending:  σ<sub>b</sub> = 32M/(πd³) = 32 × 1.2 × 10⁶/(π × 125,000) = 97.78 MPa
Axial:    σ<sub>a</sub> = F/A = 10,000/1963.5 = 5.09 MPa (compression)
Torsion:  τ = 16T/(πd³) = 16 × 572,958/(π × 125,000) = 23.34 MPa

answer.text: Worst point. The thrust is compressive, so it adds to the bending compression. On the compression side σx = −97.78 − 5.09 = −102.88 MPa; on the tension side σx = 97.78 − 5.09 = 92.69 MPa. Take σx = −102.88 MPa, σy = 0, τxy = 23.34 MPa.
Principal stresses:
answer.pre:
centre = σ<sub>x</sub>/2 = −51.44 MPa
radius = √(51.44² + 23.34²) = 56.49 MPa
σ₁ = −51.44 + 56.49 = 5.05 MPa
σ₂ = −51.44 − 56.49 = −107.93 MPa
τ<sub>max</sub> = 56.49 MPa
check: σ₁ + σ₂ = −102.88 = σ<sub>x</sub> + σ<sub>y</sub>  ✓

answer.text: Angle: |tan 2θp| = 2τ/|σx − σy| = 46.69/102.88 = 0.454, so 2θp = 24.4° and the principal planes are at 12.2° and 102.2° to the shaft axis. Because σx is the larger compression, σ₂ = −107.93 MPa acts on the plane nearer the axis direction (12.2°) and σ₁ on the other.
Mohr's circle (σ to the right, τ up): x face at (−102.88, 23.34), y face at (0, −23.34), centre −51.44, radius 56.49.

svg.aria: Mohr circle centred at minus 51.44 megapascals with radius 56.49, meeting the sigma axis at 5.05 and minus 107.93; the x face is at minus 102.88, 23.34 and the y face at 0, minus 23.34.

answer.text: Assumption. Transverse shear from the bending load is ignored: it is zero at the outer fibre, where σx is largest, so it does not change the principal stresses there.

Tension side, for comparison: σx = 92.69 MPa gives σ₁ = 46.35 + 51.89 = 98.24 MPa, σ₂ = −5.55 MPa, τmax = 51.89 MPa. The compression side has the larger maximum shear (56.49 against 51.89 MPa), so for a ductile shaft it is the critical point; for a brittle one the tension side, with σ₁ = 98.24 MPa, would be checked.

Use of the result. These principal stresses feed a theory of failure: by the maximum shear stress theory a shaft steel with Syt = 300 MPa would have a factor of safety of 300/(2 × 56.49) = 2.66 at this point.
Answer: at the worst point σ₁ = 5.05 MPa, σ₂ = −107.93 MPa, τmax = 56.49 MPa, principal planes at 12.2° and 102.2° to the shaft axis.

bank.q: An offset link carries a pull of 15 kN whose line of action is 60 mm from the centroid of the link's critical section. The section is rectangular, t wide and 3t deep, bending about the axis parallel to t. The allowable tensile stress is 80 MPa. Find t, round it up to a whole millimetre, and give the stresses at both edges of the chosen section.
outline: A and Z in terms of t
direct plus bending stress
equation for t and its solution
round up and recheck
stress on the far edge

answer.text: Section in terms of t:
answer.pre:
A = t × 3t = 3t²
Z = b h²/6 = t (3t)²/6 = 1.5t³

answer.text: Loads on the section. The offset force is replaced by a force P = 15,000 N at the centroid plus a couple M = Pe = 15,000 × 60 = 900,000 N·mm.
Maximum tensile stress on the edge nearer the load line, where direct and bending tension add:
Solve 5000/t² + 600,000/t³ = 80 by trial:

t = 20.64 mm is the least value. Round up to a whole millimetre: t = 21 mm would give 5000/441 + 600,000/9261 = 11.34 + 64.79 = 76.13 MPa. To leave room for the casting or forging tolerance a designer may take the next preferred size, 22 mm; both are acceptable answers if justified.
Chosen section 21 mm × 63 mm.
answer.pre:
A = 3 × 21² = 1323 mm²,  Z = 1.5 × 21³ = 13,892 mm³
σ<sub>direct</sub> = 15,000/1323 = 11.34 MPa
σ<sub>bending</sub> = 900,000/13,892 = 64.79 MPa
near edge: 11.34 + 64.79 = 76.13 MPa (tension) ≤ 80  ✓
far edge:  11.34 − 64.79 = −53.45 MPa (compression)

answer.text: Comment. Without the offset the stress would be only 11.34 MPa; the 60 mm offset multiplies it by 6.7. That is why links are made straight where possible, and why the bending term dominates the design of offset links and C-frames.

Assumptions. The link is straight at the critical section (an offset link has its bend elsewhere), so the straight-beam formula applies; the shear from the load is negligible; and the bending is about the axis parallel to t, which uses the deep 3t dimension and gives the smaller stress. If the link were turned the other way, Z would be 3t × t²/6 = 0.5t³ and the bending stress three times larger.
Answer: t ≥ 20.64 mm; with t = 21 mm (section 21 × 63 mm) the stresses are 76.13 MPa tension at the near edge and 53.45 MPa compression at the far edge.

bank.q: The critical section of a crane hook is a trapezium with an inner width of 60 mm, an outer width of 30 mm and a depth of 90 mm. The inner radius is 60 mm and the hook carries 30 kN on a line through the centre of curvature. Find the resultant stresses at the inner and outer fibres.
outline: area and centroid of the trapezium
R<sub>n</sub> from the trapezium formula and e
moment PR and direct stress
inner and outer bending stress with signs
resultant stresses and check

answer.text: Data: bi = 60 mm, bo = 30 mm, h = 90 mm, Ri = 60 mm, Ro = 150 mm, P = 30,000 N.
Area and centroid:
answer.pre:
A = ½(b<sub>i</sub> + b<sub>o</sub>)h = ½(60 + 30) × 90 = 4050 mm²
ȳ from inner face = h(b<sub>i</sub> + 2b<sub>o</sub>)/[3(b<sub>i</sub> + b<sub>o</sub>)] = 90 × 120/270 = 40.0 mm
R = R<sub>i</sub> + ȳ = 60 + 40 = 100.0 mm

answer.text: Neutral axis:
Moment and direct stress:
Bending stresses from σb = M(Rn − r)/(A·e·r):
Resultant stresses:

Checks. The neutral axis (93.53 mm) lies 6.47 mm inside the centroid (100 mm), toward the centre of curvature, as it must, and the inner fibre carries the larger stress. With the same area as a 45 mm × 90 mm rectangle (Rn = 90/ln 2.5 = 98.22 mm, R = 105 mm, e = 6.78 mm, M = 3.15 × 10⁶ N·mm) the inner bending stress would be 3.15 × 10⁶ × 38.22/(4050 × 6.78 × 60) = 73.1 MPa, about 14 % higher: the trapezium puts metal where the tension is.

Factor of safety. For a hook steel with Syt = 300 MPa the actual factor at the inner fibre is 300/71.35 = 4.2, which suits lifting gear, whose codes ask for large factors because a hook may be jerked.
Answer: inner fibre 71.35 MPa tension, outer fibre 35.67 MPa compression. The inner fibre, at the throat of the hook, is the critical point and the place to inspect for cracks in service.

bank.q: A hollow steel shaft with inner diameter 0.6 times the outer transmits 20 kW at 300 rpm. The shear stress must not exceed 45 MPa and the twist must not exceed 0.25° per metre; G = 80 GPa. Find the outer and inner diameters, and compare the mass with a solid shaft of the same stiffness.
outline: torque
strength size with (1 − k⁴)
stiffness size
choose the larger, standard size, recheck
solid shaft of equal stiffness and mass ratio

answer.text: Torque:
Hollow section with k = di/do = 0.6:
Strength:
Stiffness: θ = 0.25° = 4.363 × 10⁻³ rad over L = 1000 mm, and θ = 32TL/[πGdo⁴(1 − k⁴)]:
Stiffness governs. Take d<sub>o</sub> = 70 mm, so d<sub>i</sub> = 0.6 × 70 = 42 mm.
Recheck:
Solid shaft of the same stiffness (θ ≤ 0.25°/m):

Why stiffness governs. Strength needs do ≥ 43.6 mm but stiffness 68.0 mm. The twist limit of 0.25° per metre keeps gears and couplings on a long line shaft in step; at the strength size the shaft would twist (68.0/43.6)⁴ = 5.9 times more than allowed, about 1.5° per metre.

Hollow against solid of equal strength: a solid shaft for τ ≤ 45 MPa would need d³ ≥ 16 × 636,620/(π × 45) = 72,050, d ≥ 41.6 mm; the hollow strength size (43.6 mm outside, 26.2 mm inside) weighs (43.6² − 26.2²)/41.6² = 0.70 of it. Either way a hollow shaft saves about 30 % of the mass, at the cost of boring the bore.
Answer: do = 70 mm, di = 42 mm, set by stiffness; the shear stress is only 10.9 MPa. The hollow shaft weighs about 73 % of a solid shaft of equal stiffness, because the core contributes little to J.

bank.q: Design the critical section of a crane hook for a load of 50 kN. The section is rectangular with depth twice the width (h = 2b), the inner radius is 50 mm, and the load line passes through the centre of curvature. The hook steel has S<sub>yt</sub> = 360 MPa and the factor of safety is 3. Find b, then compare with the size a designer would get from the straight-beam formula.
outline: allowable stress from n
R<sub>n</sub>, e and stresses as functions of b
trial solution for b
round up and recheck both fibres
straight-beam size and why it is unsafe

answer.text: Allowable stress: σallow = Syt/n = 360/3 = 120 MPa. The hook is ductile steel and the load is steady, so yield governs; the factor of 3 also covers the shock of lifting.
Section in terms of b: h = 2b, Ro = 50 + 2b, A = 2b², R = 50 + b, Rn = 2b/ln[(50 + 2b)/50], e = R − Rn, M = P·R = 50,000(50 + b). The inner fibre carries σ = P/A + M(Rn − 50)/(A·e·50).
Trial values (because Rn depends on b, solve by trial):
So b ≥ 46.3 mm. Round up to b = 48 mm, h = 96 mm.
Recheck at b = 48 mm:

Straight-beam design for comparison: σ = P/A + M/Z with Z = b(2b)²/6 = (2/3)b³. At b = 40 mm: 50,000/3200 + 4.5 × 10⁶/42,667 = 15.6 + 105.5 = 121.1 MPa; at b = 41 mm: 14.87 + 99.03 = 113.9 MPa. A straight-beam designer would choose b of about 41 mm.

Evaluation. At b = 41 mm the true curved-beam inner stress is 157.7 MPa, so the real factor of safety would be 360/157.7 = 2.28 instead of 3. The straight-beam formula is unsafe for a hook because h/R is large (96/98 ≈ 1); the curved-beam formula raises the size from 41 to 48 mm.

Shank check. The straight shank above the bend carries only the direct pull: a round shank of 40 mm (1257 mm²) would work at 50,000/1257 = 39.8 MPa, far below 120 MPa, so the bend, not the shank, sets the size.
Answer: b = 48 mm, h = 96 mm; inner fibre 110.9 MPa tension, outer fibre 38.0 MPa compression, actual factor of safety 3.25. In practice a trapezoidal section, wider at the inside, would save mass.

bank.q: A cast-iron punch-press frame has a rectangular curved section 50 mm wide and 120 mm deep with an inner radius of 80 mm. The punching force of 25 kN acts 200 mm from the centre of curvature. The cast iron has S<sub>ut</sub> = 240 MPa and the required factor of safety is 3. A checker used the straight-beam formula and passed the frame. Evaluate the frame and, if needed, find a new width.
outline: straight-beam check the checker did
curved-beam R<sub>n</sub>, e, M = P(a + R)
inner and outer resultant stresses
true factor of safety and verdict
new width with the same depth

answer.text: Allowable stress: cast iron is brittle, so σallow = Sut/n = 240/3 = 80 MPa in tension.
Section and moment:
The checker's straight-beam check:
Curved-beam check:
Resultant stresses:

Verdict. The true tensile stress at the throat is 104.0 MPa, 39 % above the straight-beam value, and the factor of safety is 240/104.0 = 2.31, below the required 3. The frame fails the check. The outer compression (49.9 MPa) is no problem: cast iron is about three to four times stronger in compression than in tension. The error came from using a straight-beam formula on a section whose depth (120 mm) is almost the centroidal radius (140 mm).
New width. With h and the radii unchanged, Rn and e do not depend on b, and every stress varies as 1/b. The width that brings the inner stress to 80 MPa is:

Other remedies. Increasing the inner radius also helps, because it lowers the curvature: a larger Ri moves the result toward the straight-beam value. Increasing the depth helps most, since the bending stress falls roughly as 1/h², but it changes the frame's outline and the throat clearance of the press.
Answer: the frame is unsafe (n = 2.31); widening the section to 66 mm restores n = 3.05. A T or I section with the flange at the throat would do the same with less metal.

bank.q: A hand lever is a cantilever 300 mm long with a square section of side a and an end load of 500 N. It must have a factor of safety of 2 on yield and an end deflection of at most 1 mm. Compare mild steel (S<sub>yt</sub> 250 MPa, E 200 GPa, 7850 kg/m³, ₹60/kg), aluminium alloy 6061-T6 (276 MPa, 69 GPa, 2700 kg/m³, ₹300/kg) and alloy steel (650 MPa, 200 GPa, 7850 kg/m³, ₹120/kg), and recommend one.
outline: bending moment and Z, I of a square
side a for strength in each material
side a for stiffness in each material
governing size, mass and cost
recommendation and why alloy steel does not help

answer.text: Loads and section: root moment M = FL = 500 × 300 = 150,000 N·mm; for a square of side a, Z = a³/6 and I = a⁴/12.
Strength: σ = M/Z = 6M/a³ ≤ Syt/2, so a ≥ (12M/Syt)1/3.
answer.pre:
mild steel:  (1.8 × 10⁶/250)<sup>1/3</sup> = 19.31 mm
aluminium:   (1.8 × 10⁶/276)<sup>1/3</sup> = 18.68 mm
alloy steel: (1.8 × 10⁶/650)<sup>1/3</sup> = 14.04 mm

answer.text: Stiffness: δ = FL³/(3EI) = 4FL³/(Ea⁴) ≤ 1 mm, so a ≥ (4FL³/E)1/4.
Governing size, mass and cost (mass = ρa²L):

Analysis. Stiffness governs in all three. Alloy steel is far stronger, but its E is the same as mild steel's, so it needs the same 22.80 mm section and simply costs twice as much: strength bought and not used. Aluminium is 41 % lighter, because for a stiff beam the merit index is √E/ρ (√200/7.85 = 1.80 against √69/2.70 = 3.08), but it costs nearly three times as much as mild steel.

Check of the stresses at the chosen size: steel at 22.80 mm: σ = 6 × 150,000/22.80³ = 75.9 MPa, actual n = 250/75.9 = 3.29; aluminium at 29.74 mm: σ = 34.2 MPa, n = 8.1. Both are well inside the strength limit, confirming that stiffness sets the size.
Check of the deflection at a = 23 mm for mild steel: I = 23⁴/12 = 23,320 mm⁴; δ = 500 × 300³/(3 × 200,000 × 23,320) = 0.965 mm ≤ 1 mm ✓; stress = 6 × 150,000/23³ = 74.0 MPa, n = 3.38.
Rounding. The governing 22.80 mm is rounded up to the next whole size, 23 mm for steel and 30 mm for aluminium; rounding down would break the deflection limit, because the deflection grows as 1/a⁴.

Recommendation. For a hand lever on a machine, mass hardly matters and cost does: choose mild steel, 23 mm square (1.22 kg, about ₹73). Choose aluminium only where mass matters, as on a vehicle or a portable tool. Never choose alloy steel for a stiffness-limited part.

glossary.def: The planned difference between the smallest hole and the largest shaft: the minimum clearance, or if negative the maximum interference.
The highest working stress permitted: the material strength divided by the factor of safety.
The size named on the drawing, from which the limits are set by the deviations.
A material that breaks with little plastic deformation (elongation below about 5 %), such as grey cast iron.
A fit in which the hole is never smaller than the shaft, so there is always a gap or zero clearance.
A member curved before loading, whose bending stress varies hyperbolically across the depth.
A published, enforceable set of design rules for safety: load cases, methods, minimum factors and tests.
A material that deforms plastically before breaking (elongation above about 5 %), such as mild steel.
A load whose line of action does not pass through the centroid of the section, giving direct stress plus bending.
The ratio of the failure stress (yield or ultimate strength) to the allowable stress.
The deviation of a tolerance zone nearer the basic size; its letter places the zone.
A system of fits in which every hole has zero lower deviation (H) and the shaft is varied.
A large force acting for a very short time, as when one body strikes another.
A fit in which the shaft is always larger than the hole, so the parts must be pressed or shrunk together.
The number of an international tolerance grade (IT01 to IT18) that sets the width of a tolerance zone.
A graphical construction giving the normal and shear stresses on every plane at a point, and the principal stresses.
The line in a bent section where the bending stress is zero.
Z<sub>p</sub> = J/(d/2), equal to πd³/16 for a solid shaft.
Standard values in geometric series (R5, R10, R20, R40) used for sizes and ratings.
A normal stress on a plane that carries no shear stress; the largest and smallest normal stresses at a point.
The strain energy a material stores elastically, S<sub>yt</sub>²/(2E) per unit volume at yield.
Z = I/c, the ratio of the second moment of area to the distance of the outer fibre.
The difference between the upper and lower limits of a size.
The energy a material absorbs before fracture.
A fit whose tolerance zones overlap, so a pair may have a small clearance or a small interference.
A way of ranking materials by scaling each property out of 100, weighting it and adding the scores.
